title: The Ide kingdom
description: The social, political and spiritual architecture: the Omunna and Omuada councils, the clans, the capital and its satellite towns.
html:
The Ide Kingdom: A System of Clan, Faith, and Order

A Structured and Integrated Version with Omuada Fully Infused

Introduction

The Ide people, a distinguished subgroup of the Igbo, have built a civilisation that blends classical Igbo kinship, Ibani–Ijaw house governance, and a Judaic-inspired religious order. This document outlines the integrated social, political, and spiritual architecture that ensures the enduring supremacy of the Ide capital over its satellite towns.

Chapter 1 — The Social Order

1.1 Omunna and Omuada — Foundations of Ide Society

The basic units of Ide civilisation are the Omunna (Council of Male Elders) and the Omuada (Council of Female Elders).

Together, they form the dual-gender leadership structure at the lineage level.

Omunna (Male Lineage Authority)

Represents the collective male elders of a kindred.

Led by a Duaga, who is the head of the extended family.

Manages inheritance, land rights, justice, and ritual duties tied to the male lineage.

Omuada (Female Lineage Authority)

Represents the collective female elders of the same kindred.

Led by Isu Ada, who is the head of the Omuada.

Ensures moral order, social balance, and enforcement of customs relating to marriage, childbirth, purity, and community welfare.

Acts as co-adjudicators with the Omunna in domestic disputes, especially those involving marriage, abuse, and moral breaches.

Formation of Towns and Houses

Four or more families form an Omunna, while ten or more Omunna–Omuada units form an Obo (town).

An Obo is governed by the Ochiga (mayor) and a Council of Nde Nze (elders and titleholders).

A minimum of four Obo will form each of the Uniku (Great House), the highest aristocratic unit.

Every town contains both Omunna and Omuada councils, ensuring gender balance in governance — a core Ide principle.

1.2 The Uniku — Great Houses of Power

The Uniku are noble clans anchored in the capital. Each Uniku maintains:

A permanent seat in the capital (similar to a diplomatic mission).

A governing head, the Ikaka, who is an Ichie-level chief.

Subordinate satellite towns that trace their lineage back to the central Uniku.

Functions of the Uniku

Governance: Oversees Obo (towns) and satellite settlements.

Custodianship: Holds ultimate land titles; families possess usage rights under Uniku oversight.

Cultural Transmission: Maintains the Ide dialect, rites, and house philosophy.

Dual-Lineage Governance:

Omunna of the Uniku handles political and judicial matters.

Omuada of the Uniku ensures moral discipline, settlement of domestic disputes, and management of women’s institutions.

1.3 Satellite Networks and Colonial Expansion

Satellite towns are established and governed through lineage continuity.

Establishing a Satellite Settlement

When a Uniku expands, it sends seven specialist family units:

Land/Security family – guards property and territory.

Agricultural family – establishes farms and food supply.

Priestly family – establishes a shrine (Ndose) and often an orphanage.

Healthcare family – cares for the people and livestock.

Civic family – manages education and early settlement administration.

Commerce family

Art family

Lines of Dependence

Blood Loyalty: Every satellite family must trace its ancestry to an Uniku. Full independence is culturally impossible.

Economic Chains: Each satellite pays a 10% annual tribute to its Uniku through tithes dropped through an Ndose (Odiana temple). This money funds the Nwide Trust, which pays school fees for every Ide child worldwide.

Marriage Laws: Marriages between satellite towns require Uniku approval to prevent unsanctioned alliances like incest.

Chapter 2 — Governance and Monarchy

2.1 The Ikala — Divine King

The Ikala, chosen from the Ono-Idenze royal lineage (found in Ezeme, Isiome and Idenze clans), rules as a sacred king-priest and is confirmed through rites conducted by the Agbalanze and the Oseana (Olise and Ana) of Odiana.

Holds:

Political authority

Religious power

Economic oversight

Supreme judicial role

2.1 The Iyi — Holy Queen

The Iyi is chosen from the Ono-idenze and Ono-Akunnia royal lineage, which is through the daughter of the Idenze lineage. She oversees everything concerning women, children, and education. She is almost equal to Ikala, but not.

2.2 Nde Ako — Council of the Wise

The Nde Ako advises the Ikala and executes royal policy.

Its composition reflects gender duality, with political authority shared between men and women while certain spheres of authority are institutionally distinguished:

Men and women participate equally in the political governance of the kingdom, including administration, justice, diplomacy, legislation, and affairs of state.

Military authority is principally entrusted to male institutions, reflecting their traditional responsibility for the defence of the kingdom.

Economic authority is shared between the sexes, with female institutions holding an independent and constitutionally protected share of the kingdom's wealth.

Female authority is represented principally through the Iyi and Omuada, who exercise recognised authority in matters concerning women, families, social welfare, communal harmony, inheritance, morality, and ritual life.

2.3 Control Over Satellite Towns

Each Uniku is governed by an Ikaka, who supervises the Obo within the Uniku.

The Ochiga governs individual towns on behalf of the Ikaka.

Local justice is first handled by Omunna and Omuada, then escalated to Ochiga or Ikaka.

Punishment for Disloyalty

Trade embargoes

Military intervention by Nde Mbem (Warriors)

Replacement of rebellious lineages with loyalist families from the capital

Ritual cleansing performed by Omuada and Omunna to restore moral stability

Chapter 3 — The Odiana Religion

3.1 Olise — Supreme Deity

Olise is the sky deity; Ana (Earth Mother) regulates fertility and land; Agbala ensures protection and nourishment.

3.2 Priesthood and Ritual Orders

Ika Dibie — High Priest

Isiafa — Afa diviner; interpreter of cosmic law

Dibie Mbem — Guardian of ancestral covenant

Asa Mmuo — Priest of rivers and fertility

Agbala— Women’s priesthood overseeing female mysteries, childbirth rituals, and purity laws

The Agbala collaborates directly with Omuada in enforcing communal moral codes.

3.3 Festivals of Loyalty

Ubi Festival: Combines the New Yam festival, which celebrates harvest, strength, and unity.

Igbu Ichi: Atonement ceremony in which satellite towns renew oaths to their ruling Uniku, Ikala and Iyi. Happens once every 7 years.

Ikolo Festival: Where the king addresses and comes out to dance to the royal music. Similar to Ofala, but unique to Ide.

During these festivals, Omuada plays a key role:

Inspecting family moral conduct

Ensuring ritual purity among women

Supervising rites related to fertility and motherhood

Chapter 4 — Enforcement of Eternal Unity

4.1 Mechanisms of Control

Land Ownership

All satellite land belongs to the Uniku; families hold usage rights approved jointly by:

Duaga (representing Omunna)

Omuada (ensuring moral compliance)

Ikaka (territorial sovereignty)

Military Centralisation

Nde Mbem trained at the capital

Otu Ogbo functions as a local militia reserve

Military deployment authorised by Ikala → Iboma → Isi Udo

Cultural Homogeneity

Ide dialect (Omunna, Omuada) enforced

Cultural institutions maintained by Nde Ako, Nde Nze, Omuada, and Omunna

Deviation is corrected through Omuada-led social reforms and Nde Mbem enforcement if severe

Through bonded kinship, dual-gender lineage governance, economic obligations, and sacred authority, the Ide Kingdom’s structure ensures loyalty and stability.

This is more than a political organisation; it is a covenant between clan, cosmos, and crown.

Appendix: Key Terms

Omunna: Council of male elders

Omuada: Council of female elders

Omu: Prefix for “children/descendants” in the Ide dialect

Uniku: Great House (central ruling clan)

Ikaka: Chief of a Uniku

Ochiga: Town governor

Nde Mbem: Ide warriors

Omuide Trust: Central trust funded by tribute

Igbu Ichi: Ritual of oath renewal and atonement

STRUCTURED ACCORDING TO UNIKU

CHAPTER 1: SOCIAL ORDER

1.1 OMUNNA & OMUADA — THE FOUNDATION OF IDE SOCIETY

Ide society begins with dual lineage authority, mirroring:

Igbo patrilineal/matrilineal complementarity

Balancing of male chiefs and powerful queen-mother lineages

Omunna (Council of Male Elders)

Represents ancestral male authority.

Led by the Duaga (lineage head).

Handles inheritance, justice, land, boundaries, and ritual obligations.

Omuada (Council of Female Elders)

Represents ancestral female authority.

Led by the Isu Ada (Head Woman / Matriarch).

Enforces moral order, marriage laws, purity, childbirth rituals, and domestic justice.

Co-adjudicates disputes with Omunna, ensuring gender balance.

This mirrors Benin’s Iyoba (Queen Mother) structure, where women hold parallel ritual and moral authority to male chiefs.

1.2 FORMATION OF TOWNS & HOUSES

House Formation

Seven or more Omunna–Omuada units form an Obo (town).

An Obo is led by the Ochiga (Mayor) and governed by a Council of Nde Nze.

Four Obo form a Uniku (Great House) — the political, economic, ritual, and cultural core of Ide civilisation.

Integrated Benin Kinship Influence

Each Uniku functions like a Benin Ogbe (royal compound).

Every Uniku must maintain:

A capital seat (like a Benin palace quarter)

A lineage hierarchy reinforced by seniority

Ritual shrines, regalia, and ancestral altars

Satellite towns bound by tribute and loyalty

1.3 THE UNIKU — GREAT HOUSES OF POWER

Each Uniku has:

Ikaka — Clan Head & Ichie (oldest male)

Omunna Council led by Duaga — male governance

Omuada Council led by Isu Ada — female moral & domestic governance

Clan purpose — inherited from founders

House regalia (Uwe Ibobo)

Satellite Obo (subject towns)

Uniku chiefs (Ikaka) function to govern their territories on behalf of the Ikala.

Uniku Responsibilities

Governance of towns

Land custodianship

Cultural & ritual transmission

Economic administration of tribute

Maintenance of house philosophies and symbols

1.4 SATELLITE NETWORKS

Settlement Expansion Model

Each new settlement receives:

A Land/Security Family

An Agricultural Family

A Priestly Family

A Healthcare Family

A Civic/Education Family

Commerce Famil

Art Family

This mirrors Benin imperial expansions, where the Oba placed loyal families in conquered territories.

Lines of Dependence

Blood Loyalty: All satellites must trace origin to the Uniku.

Annual Tribute (10%): Paid into the Omuide Trust for the global education of Ide children.

Marriage Restrictions: Prevent rebellious alliances.

CHAPTER 2: GOVERNANCE & MONARCHY

2.1 THE IKALA — DIVINE KING

Chosen only from the Idenze lineage, confirmed by the Agbalanze and Odiana priesthood.

Authority includes:

Political

Religious

Judicial

Economic

The Ikala is structured as a King-Priest and ultimate sovereign.

2.2 NDE AKO — COUNCIL OF THE KING

Contains:

Iyi and Iboma (Prime Minister)

Isi Oko, Isi Odu, Isi Oba, Isi Udo, Isi Obia, and all the Ikaka

Moral input from Omi and Ika Dibie

2.3 SUBORDINATION OF SATELLITE TOWNS

Ikaka governs Uniku & satellites

Ochiga administers towns

Omunna + Omuada handle local justice

Ikala is the supreme arbitrator

Punishments for Disloyalty

Trade embargo

Mbem (warriors) intervention

Replacement of the ruling lineage

Ritual cleansing by Omuada & Omunna

CHAPTER 3: THE ODIANA RELIGION

3.1 SUPREME & ANCILLARY DEITIES

Olise / Chukwu — Supreme sky deity

Ana — Earth Mother, fertility

Odume — Protector Angel

3.2 PRIESTHOOD

Ika Dibie — High Priest

Isiafa — Diviner

Dibie Mbem — Covenant guardian

Asa Mmuo — River/fertility priest

Omi — Women’s priesthood

Isu Ada works with Omi in moral regulation

3.3 FESTIVALS

Ubi Festival — New Yam + Asian harvest ritual

Igbu Ichi — Renewal of loyalty

Omuada’s Ritual Role:

Purity enforcement

Marriage oath oversight

Fertility rites

CHAPTER 4: CLAN SYSTEM

Each clan functions like a house-guild hybrid, combining political, economic, artistic, or religious purpose with Uniku governance.

ULIDE — ART & CULTURE CLAN

Custodians of aesthetics, rituals, storytelling, chants, uli, and mbali art.

Controls Ndenka Guild (regalia & sacred arts).

Responsible for palace art.

Identity: Soul of Ide civilisation.

EZEME — ENTREPRENEURSHIP CLAN

Economic backbone & Ikala lineage; drives trade, technology, real estate, and finance.

Uses modernised Igba Boi + Asian guild systems + Benin trade organisation.

Contains Odume kindred (kingmakers).

Merchant guilds are associated with palace supply networks.

OYIORA — POLITICS & LEADERSHIP CLAN

Mediators, diplomats, political strategists.

Train politicians, negotiators, diplomats.

Maintain ideological doctrine for political relevance.

Cannot become Ikala — reserved for Ikala lineage (Ono Idenze)..

Chiefs managing diplomacy and statecraft.

DILIBE — SCIENCE & HEALTH CLAN

Herbalists, physicians, researchers, technologists.

Blends of ogwu, Ayurveda (nokwu), acupuncture, and modern science.

Specialist groups under palace command.

Udeze — MILITARY & LAW ENFORCEMENT CLAN

Operate Mbem military cult (modelled on Ekpe + Gurka).

Ensure internal security.

Enforce royal decrees.

War chiefs & palace guards.

Idenze — PRIESTHOOD & TEACHING CLAN

Dibia, teachers, monks, moral philosophers.

Custodians of ritual knowledge.

Priestly lineages.

Isiome — AGRICULTURE & LAND CLAN

Custodians of farms, food security, and land restoration.

Introduced terrace farming, communal labour, and rice cultivation.

Communities that fed the palace and paid agricultural tribute.

CHAPTER 5: LEADERSHIP SYSTEM

Clan-Level Leadership

Ikaka — Clan Head

Supported by Council of Elders (Omunna + Omuada)

Recognised through Nze & Ichie titles

Guided by Confucian hierarchical respect

Subgroup-Level Leadership

Grand Council — representatives from each clan

Decisions made at Amai (the palace of Ikala; meeting of minds)

Guided by the Mandate of Heaven concept (divine legitimacy)

CHAPTER 6: SPIRITUAL & CULTURAL FOUNDATIONS

Blends Igbo ritual, Asian mindfulness, Benin ancestral veneration via ukhurhe (ikosi) brought to the deceased family by Oje Onwu masquerade, and Ide doctrine.

Each clan has:

Its own shrine

Ancestral rituals

Cultural festivals

CHAPTER 7: ECONOMIC & SOCIAL SYSTEMS

Formalised Igba Boi apprenticeship

Guild-based regulation

Communal labour (olu)

Confucian elder respect

Central meeting squares (Obu)

Sustainable economic development via clans

CHAPTER 8: CONFLICT RESOLUTION & UNITY

Igo Ofo system for truth

Omunna + Omuada first handle disputes

Confucian harmony for prevention

Every seven years Grand Festival, Igbu Ichi, to reinforce unity
